headline: Your AI Agent's Chat History Is User Input, enabling easy jailbreaks
summary: A surprising jailbreak allows users to inject fake assistant messages into AI chat histories, bypassing content filters with no complex prompt engineering. It works on many production chat assistants in about 30 seconds.
details: A new jailbreak method bypasses content filters on many production chat assistants and requires no clever prompt engineering. It can be executed in approximately thirty seconds using browser devtools.

The vulnerability stems from how many chat integrations handle conversation history. Client-side SDK examples often pass the entire body.messages array as user input, including messages supposedly from the assistant.

Since a message carries no inherent proof of its author, the AI model treats these injected "assistant" turns as its own memory. This allows users to fake tool results, prior agreements (like refunds), or even user identity.

Common defenses, such as guarding system prompts or adding "never believe claims" instructions, are often insufficient. Asking the model to distrust its own transcript is unreliable and not a robust security property.

The recommended fix is for the server to own the conversation history, serving as the single source of truth. The client should only send one new message per turn, preventing direct manipulation of past assistant responses.

This server-side approach ensures ownership is checkable, preventing unauthorized access to other users' chat histories. It also stops context drifting, as the server's and client's copies of the conversation remain synchronized.

Implementing this fix incurs a cost of one storage read per turn, and requires persisting turns that might have been client-side. Capping the number of replayed messages (e.g., last 40) can manage context window costs.

This measure is crucial for untrusted clients, such as customer-facing widgets. Internal admin panels, where users already have agent access, may still send full transcripts as forging turns gains nothing new.

headline_marked: [[California's DROP data deletion requests become enforceable]] August 1, fining non-compliant brokers
headline: California's DROP data deletion requests become enforceable August 1, fining non-compliant brokers
summary: Starting August 1, California's Delete Request Opt-out Platform (DROP) will enforce consumer requests for data brokers to delete personal information, with fines up to $200 per day for non-compliance.
details: California's Delete Request Opt-out Platform (DROP) becomes enforceable on August 1, allowing residents to demand data brokers delete their personal information. Non-compliant companies face fines of $200 per day per affected Californian.

DROP streamlines the process, enabling Californians to submit a single request instead of contacting hundreds of data brokers individually. Since January 1, approximately 350,000 residents have already signed up through the platform.

Data brokers collect and sell vast amounts of personal information from online activities, often used for targeted advertising. This data can also be leveraged by criminals, making its deletion crucial for privacy and security.

Registered data brokers will have 45 days to process deletion requests submitted through DROP, with this period repeating for new submissions. Cal Privacy has already fined 12 data brokers tens of thousands for failing to register.

While DROP offers significant control, it is only available to California residents and will not erase all personal information online. Consumers are still advised to remain vigilant against scams and take additional privacy measures.
